newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Airport oddities.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Airport oddities.

text.p: Passengers waiting to board a recent flight from Chicago to Vancouver, Canada, were asked if someone could give up a seat so more fuel could be loaded on.
Trading passengers for fuel? It sounds like a seaplane flight into the Alaska bush.
But it's not as unusual as it sounds, according to Joe Hopkins, spokesman for United Airlines, the carrier involved in this particular case.
What is unusual, he said, is that it was happening at the gate at the last minute.

There is a "mass gross takeoff weight," Hopkins said, and at times seats may be left empty if the pilot determines that more fuel will be needed because of headwinds, weather at the destination, the possibility of having to find an alternative airport and other factors.

Normally that is calculated ahead of time, but in this case the captain might have decided to make a last minute adjustment. The gross takeoff weight includes estimates for the weight of the average passenger plus luggage.

In this case the decision to add more fuel to the Boeing 737 meant subtracting a passenger. It appeared the airline had no trouble coming up with a volunteer -- who was offered a flight leaving less than two hours later as well as other "denied boarding" compensation.
In another airport anomaly, a reader reports that a flight from Dallas to Newark earlier this year was suddenly cancelled due to "equipment failure."
The flight was nearly empty, he adds, "and I came to learn from a couple in line that the same flight was cancelled five of the last eight times they tried to fly it.

"It seems (the carrier) has certain flights they cancel when any other flight needs a plane. I had this confirmed to me by a top (airline) official. If the public knew which flights they were they would be saved a lot of hassle."

Then suspicion that some flights are pre-designated for cancellation, especially when they are nearly empty, is a common one. In this case attempts to get the carrier involved to discuss the sitution were unproductive.

Karen Goodwin, editor-in-chief of Frequent Flyer magazine, says, says airlines in general "adamantly deny that they do this" while many passengers remain sceptical, preferring to believe that "mechanical failure" is a euphemism for combining flights.

One curb on the practice, she points out, is that holding back a piece of equipment or switching it to another route can disrupt a system since aircraft are constantly in use. A failure to arrive disrupts the next leg scheduled for that piece of equipment.
In terms of finding out which flights might be cancellation-prone, one possible clue is the on-time statistical information compiled by the government.

Cancelled flights affect on-time performance ratings, according to officials at the Transportation Department's Bureau of Aviation Statistics. Federal regulations require airline reservation clerks and travel agents to disclose the on-time performance of any particular flight if the customer asks for it when booking a ticket.

A spokeswoman for Carlson Wagonlit Travel said any agent with access to a computer reservation system should be able to provide the on-time performance for a specific flight, listed as a percentage, for the previous month.
Some of the same information should be available on the DOT's Internet site at www.bts.gov. However, our recent attempt to dig it out proved time-consuming.
